background.definition: An epidermoid cyst is the most common cutaneous cyst, derived from epidermis or the epithelium of the hair follicle. It occurs mainly in areas where there are small hair follicles and larger sebaceous glands, such as the face, neck, upper trunk, genitals, and groin. It is sometimes called an epidermal inclusion cyst or a sebaceous cyst, but "epidermoid cyst" is the preferred term.

list.listitem: Epidermoid cysts are known to be very common, but reliable incidence data are not available.
Epidermoid cysts occur in young-to-middle-aged adults and may cause aesthetic problems.
Most epidermoid cysts form when epidermal cells move deeper into the skin and multiply (instead of exfoliating normally).
Factors that lead to an abnormal proliferation of cells include the blockage of a hair follicle by skin cells when damage to the skin occurs by injuries such as abrasions or surgical wounds.
Sebaceous glands ruptured by inflammatory skin conditions, especially acne, make them a likely site for cysts.
Cysts can begin as a developmental defect in a fetus when stem cells intended to form skin, hair, or nails become trapped in cells forming other tissues.

An epidermoid cyst is a benign slow-growing skin growth that results from injury to a hair follicle in association with acne, from a defect in the skin, or from injury to the skin beneath the skin surface.
Epidermoid cyst is formed by cystic enclosure of epithelium within the dermis.
The cystic lesion is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Epidermal cells form the walls of the cyst. The cyst then becomes filled with keratin and lipid-rich debris. The cyst wall may be thin and can rupture if distended or traumatized.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Damage to a hair follicle due to acne

list.listitem: There is no easy way to prevent an epidermal cyst. If any of the cyst wall is left behind after drainage, the cyst may come back. C

An epidermoid cyst is a benign and often painless slow-growing skin growth, usually solitary but may be multiple; rupture can release a cheesy material into the skin and a reaction that produces redness, tenderness, and swelling. C
Ruptured cysts are often misdiagnosed as being infected rather than ruptured. C

Pathologic evaluation of a removed cyst is suggested if there is a history of cyst recurrence, and the cyst has an atypical appearance, is solid, immobile, frequently gets infected or irritated, is changing color, or has other unusual characteristics that suggest a more serious problem and looks suspicious for skin cancer. C

Differential.Differential_Features: It manifests as smooth, mobile, asymptomatic swelling, often in the scalp.
A benign tumor composed of fat cells that presents as a rubbery subcutaneous nodule.
A benign keratin-filled cyst usually seen in infants; a superficial, pearly white, domed lesion.
It is a skin infection involving an entire hair follicle and nearby skin tissue.
It may present as a shiny, pearly, blue-gray cystic lesion with blood vessels on the surface.
Skin cancer that usually appears as a flesh-colored, red, or blue nodule.
It appears as a lesion that has little or no color. It has an asymmetrical shape and irregular border.

list.listitem: An epidermoid cyst is a dermal-to-subcutaneous nodule that often connects with the surface by keratin-filled pores. It is round, mobile, and firm, sized from a few millimeters to several centimeters. In most cases, the diagnosis is based on the epidermoid cyst's appearance alone, after a patient notices the bump on their skin. Palpation is not very sensitive but is quite specific for the diagnosis.

The content of the cyst is a keratinaceous material, cream-colored, with a pasty consistency, and the odor of rancid cheese. Following rupture of the wall, the irritating cyst contents initiate an inflammatory reaction, enlarging the lesion, which may be painful. It may remain small for years or may grow rapidly; complications include inflammation, rupture, infection, and, rarely, skin cancer.
They commonly appear on acne-prone areas of the face, behind the ears, on the scalp, and upper trunk. They are rarely found on the fingers, palms, or soles.
Miniature epidermoid cysts (called milia) can develop in skin that is injured or scraped.
Genital epidermoid cysts can lead to painful intercourse and dysuria.
Cysts are often a cosmetic problem or a cause of embarrassment.
Palpation has good specificity but poor sensitivity; thus, palpation is helpful at ruling in epidermoid cyst (LR+ 6.6) but not at ruling it out (LR− 0.6).

Epidermoid cysts should be sent for pathologic evaluation if patients have a history of cyst recurrence. Also send cysts that have an atypical appearance are solid, immobile, or infected or have other unusual characteristics that suggest a more serious problem.

A retrospective study of inflamed epidermoid cysts showed no bacterial growth or normal skin flora for 47% of cysts. For cultures that had bacterial growth, 38% grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), 13% grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aurues (MSSA), and 8% grew Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The Infectious Disease Society of America does not recommend routine performance of gram stain and culture on pus or drainage from inflamed epidermoid cysts.

Ultrasound has moderate sensitivity and very good specificity for diagnosing epidermoid cyst, but is not always necessary. When available, point-of-care ultrasonography may help with perioperative evaluation and surgical planning.
An epidermoid cyst is a dermal-to-subcutaneous nodule that often connects with the surface by keratin-filled pores.

It is round, mobile, and firm, sized from a few millimeters to several centimeters. In most cases, the diagnosis is based on the epidermoid cyst's appearance alone, after a patient notices the bump on their skin.
Treatment is by excision, which is curative.

Pathologic evaluation of a removed cyst is suggested if there is a history of cyst recurrence or if the cyst has an atypical appearance; is solid, immobile, or frequently gets infected or irritated; is changing color; or has other unusual characteristics that suggest a more serious problem and looks suspicious for skin cancer.
Most epidermoid cysts do not cause problems or need treatment. C

For mildly inflamed epidermoid cysts, consider watchful waiting or symptomatic treatment with warm compress, NSAIDS, and intralesional corticosteroid injection. Despite the paucity of strong evidence, many primary care physicians and dermatologists prescribe oral antibiotics for inflamed epidermoid cysts. C

Perform incision and drainage for significantly inflamed, fluctuant epidermoid cysts; gram stain and culture of drainage or pus is not routinely recommended for noncomplex, immunocompetent patients. C
Surgical management of symptomatic, noninflamed epidermoid cysts include minimal incisional approach, punch technique, elliptical excision, and laser treatment. C
Corticosteroid injections may help reduce the inflammation of inflamed epidermoid cysts.

The use of antibiotics is not recommended for asymptomatic, noninflamed epidermoid cysts. Despite the paucity of strong evidence, many primary care physicans and dermatologists prescribe oral antibiotics for inflamed epidermoid cysts, with the goal of decreasing the inflammation, treating the infection (if present), and avoiding more aggressive measures. When concurrent cellulitis is present, antibiotics is indicated.

Commonly used antibiotics are those with good gram-positive coverage (for Staphylococcus and Streptococcus), including lower generation cephalosporins, penicillin derivatives, tetracyclines, clindamycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Tetracyclines, like minocycline and doxycycline, are believed to have anti-inflammatory properties which may account for improvement when treating noninfected, inflamed epidermoid cysts.
Indications for surgical intervention include a cosmetic concern, rupture of cyst, painful cyst, and recurrent infection.
The chance of recurrence is low if the entire cyst wall is removed.
Facial epidermoid cysts less than 1 cm in diameter can be successfully managed with a minimal incision to achieve minimized scarring and better cosmetic results.
Perform incision and drainage for significantly inflamed, fluctuant epidermoid cysts; gram stain and culture of drainage or pus is not routinely recommended for noncomplex, immunocompetent patients.

A small prospective, randomized study in Taiwan of 60 patients with noninflamed epidermoid cysts concluded that punch technique followed by cyst evacuation leads to smaller scars and shorter operative time compared to standard elliptical excision. Recurrence rate, complications, and patient satisfaction were similar between the two groups after 16 months. Blinding was not clearly stated in the study. Additionally, large cysts (>2 cm) treated with punch technique had similar operative times as those elliptically excised.

Serial laser treatment using the erbium:yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG) laser fenestration technique to decompress the cyst contents is an alternative to surgery that results in no scar formation. It is worth considering for large lesions or those with particular aesthetic concern.
Prognosis is usually good. Recurrence may occur if entire cyst is not removed during surgical intervention. C
Ruptured cysts can cause skin scarring and discomfort. C
